subject: Chemistry
title: Ionic Bonds: Stealing Electrons
description: A fast breakdown of Ionic Bonds: Stealing Electrons for builders.

hook.text: Table salt forms when sodium gives an electron to chlorine. The charged atoms attract and lock into a crystal.

buildup.text: Sodium has one outer electron it wants to lose. Chlorine needs one more electron to fill its outer shell.

discovery.text: Sodium becomes Na⁺ and chlorine becomes Cl⁻. The opposite charges attract with enormous force—an ionic bond.

twist.text: Ionic compounds form rigid crystal lattices, not molecules. Each Na⁺ is surrounded by six Cl⁻ ions and vice versa.

climax.text: Dissolve salt in water and the ions separate. That's why salt water conducts electricity—free ions carry the current.

punchline.text: Give an electron, take an electron, opposite charges lock together. That's salt.

quiz.question: Why does salt dissolve in water and conduct electricity?
options: Water separates Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, which carry electrical current
Salt molecules break apart into individual atoms
Water chemically reacts with salt to produce electrons

details.summary: Ionic bonds form when one atom transfers electrons to another, creating oppositely charged ions that attract each other through electrostatic force. This typically occurs between metals that lose electrons easily and nonmetals that gain them readily, producing crystalline compounds like table salt.
details.whyItMatters: Ionic bonding explains the properties of salts, ceramics, and minerals that form much of Earth's crust. Understanding it is fundamental to materials science and biological chemistry.
takeaways: Metals donate electrons to nonmetals forming cation-anion pairs
Ionic compounds form organized crystal lattice structures
They typically have high melting points and conduct electricity when dissolved

faq.question: Why do ionic compounds dissolve in water but covalent compounds often do not?
faq.answer: Water molecules are polar and can surround individual ions, pulling them away from the crystal lattice through a process called hydration. Covalent compounds lack charged particles for water to interact with strongly, so many remain insoluble unless they are also polar.

faq.question: Is the bond in sodium chloride purely ionic?
faq.answer: No bond is perfectly ionic. Even in sodium chloride, there is slight electron sharing between ions. Bonding exists on a spectrum from pure ionic to pure covalent. Electronegativity difference determines where a bond falls on this spectrum.
